newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia divided over liberation holiday.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia divided over liberation holiday.

text.p: Eighteen years after the Vietnamese invasion that toppled Cambodia's brutal Khmer Rouge regime, politicians still cannot agree on whether the event is cause for celebration or mourning.

Opinions are sharply divided about Tuesday's national holiday marking the anniversary, evidence that the fault lines from Cambodia's traumatic past still exist in today's fragile coalition government.

"I'm on holiday, but I won't be celebrating," noted one member of parliament who, as a member of co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, believes the Vietnamese invasion of January 7, 1979, was merely another sad chapter in Cambodia's history.
Ranariddh's followers fought the Vietnamese-installed regime, and their future coalition partner -- co-Premier Hun Sen -- throughout the 1980s.
Not suprisingly, Hun Sen sees it differently.
"January 7 lives on forever," Hun Sen said in a speech on Monday. "It liberated the people from the genocidal regime."
Hun Sen pushed for the re-establishment of the national holiday one year ago after it had been suspended for four years.
Hun Sen, together with Cambodian resistance fighters and Vietnamese troops, was among those who overthrew the "killing fields" regime that day in January 1979.

The Maoist Khmer Rouge guerrillas, who led a radical experiment in agrarian reform, were blamed for the deaths of more than one million Cambodians through execution, overwork, starvation, and disease.

The rebels fought Hun Sen's Hanoi-backed government for years before signing a U.N.-sponsored peace pact in 1991. But they later reneged on the deal and fought the coalition government formed following the 1993 elections.

The past year has seen the rebels decimated by waves of defections, but while their demise has brought some measure of peace in their battle with the four-year-old government, it has divided Hun Sen and Ranariddh, who have competed for control over the defectors and their territory.

The growing animosity between the two leaders, who formed their uneasy coalition after running against each other in the 1993 elections, will be exhibited by the way their supporters treat the holiday, analysts said.
"I'll be coming to work tomorrow," said a member of Ranariddh's cabinet who does not recognise the holiday.
